name: al-Jumaih
bio: Munqidh ibn at-Tammah, called al-Jumaih, was of the tribe of Asad; Lyall describes him as the son of a contemporary and enemy of Imra' al-Qais, and says that he fell at the battle of Shi'b Jabalah, fought in or about A.D. 570.
Three of his poems are in the Mufaddaliyat: a complaint against a wife set at variance with him by her people, a denunciation of a treacherous killing, and a lament for a chief.

poems.title: Ode IV: Umamah has become tongue-tied, and will
poems.author: al-Jumaih
poems.note: Lyall's heading: Munqidh son of at-Tammah, called al-Jumaih, of Asad.
poems.text:
Umamah has become tongue-tied, and will not speak a word to me : is she gone mad, or has she been taking counsel with the folk of Kharrub ?

She passed by the rider of a camel branded in the angle of the lower jaw, and he counselled her — ' Vex al-Jumaih, and assail him with annoyances.'

But if she had hit the truth, she would have said — for she is a truth-speaker — ' As for trying to train the grey-headed, trouble not thyself therewith ;

'His full age forbids it, and there forbids it the fact that your aged husband will never now submit to blows and schooling.'

But when she attacks me, then is she a [lioness] with whelps, short haired, that defends her brake so that it cannot be approached :

But if anything happens to terrify her, then is she like a child in a smock, whom thou chidest all day long, [threatening it] with the terror of the wolf.

And if her people be dwellers in Qidah, then my folk are they who dwell in Malhub.

[All this happened] when she saw that among my camels were few that yielded milk, and every year that passed over them was a year of dried-up udders.

The changes and chances of things — and they follow close upon my beasts — , and the payment of things due, have left them a little herd with a herdsman who is not overwhelmed by his charge ;

Thou wouldst think our herdsman was driving in them a troop of asses, between the pie-bald plains of Makran and the lavas of the Harrah.

But if thou lookest on us kindly, and abatest thy pride when thou comest amongst us, and regardest my valour in fight and my raids carried far abroad—

Then possess thyself in patience— it may be that yet shalt thou be happy, and milk thy herds into a great milk-skin — the skin of a sheep tanned with acacia-bark.

poems.title: Ode VII: Ask Ma'add who were the knights
poems.author: al-Jumaih
poems.text:
Ask Ma'add who were the knights who did not keep faith with those with whom they had covenanted, and yet got no booty !

Qurzul ran away with them, while men listened [to the battering of their hoofs], and the long locks fluttered, streaming in the breeze,

As they galloped away ; and they had left Rabl'ah lying among those that slew him, when the fighters were close together in the press of battle —

In his hand a lithe spear-shaft, well straightened in the clip, on it a spear-head kindled to wrath, eager for men's flesh.

If Khalid son of Nadlah had had any fear of your treachery, there had borne him away a swimmer whose reins outstrip [all other steeds that race with her] —

A mare short of hair, spare like a straightened spear : her back has not been wrinkled with the cold, nor has her food been stinted.

And al-Harith was there, shouting loud his call for help — among his companions a sure refuge and support :

There gallops with him a full-grown steed with a deep-toned neigh, that leads as their best all the horses of the tribe, stout, the heads of his long bones well covered with fat,

His rider arrayed in a fair coat of mail, woven double, sinning like a pool [smitten by a breeze], in the best part of a hollow, kept full by constant showers.

poems.title: Ode CIX: O thou protector of Nadlah, the
poems.author: al-Jumaih
poems.text:
O thou protector of Nadlah, the time, truly, has come for thee to bestir thyself in defence of thy friend among the sons of Hidm !

Ye that range yourselves one to another to shelter Nadlah — ugly your faces in that chain of protecting hands !

And the Sons of Rawahah look on, what time the assembly gaze at him with their thick fleshy noses :

Except Abu Thauban — in sooth Abu Thauban is not dumb or tongue-tied —

'Amr son of 'Abdallah — verily he is a man who holds himself aloof from reviling and foul abuse.

Give me not to drink if I bring not on Ghatafan by night the marching of a mighty and numberless host,

Clangorous when [its enemies] beset its companies on both flanks, like a lofty mass of cloud on the day of the setting-in of the heavy autumnal rain —

A host so vast that the wide plain is too strait for it, huge, with a vanguard whose dust floats hither and thither :

They shout the name of Nadlah as they thrust with the spears, bestriding short-haired steeds that spring with the gait of mountain goats —

All tall steeds and mares firmly knit, like a well-twisted cable, some bay, some black —

Until I requite upon 'Abs the wickedness they wrought with the worst that such a crime deserves.

O Nadlah ! [Alas] for the stranger guest, for the man under covenant who / is wronged, and for him who bears the burthen of heavy debt !

Who now will succour the shag-pate wretch who cannot sleep for hunger, the starveling clad in worn-out rags, lean as the camel tied to die at its master's grave ?
